segments.caption: Your friend's coin lands heads 9 times out of 10.
Is the coin rigged, or was it just luck?
Hypothesis testing helps you decide.
Here's the definition, in simple words.
Hypothesis testing uses data to decide whether an effect is real, or just chance.
First, assume nothing special is going on.
Then check: is the data too surprising for that to be true?
That gives us two hypotheses.
The null hypothesis: nothing's going on. The coin is fair.
The alternative: something is going on. The coin favours heads.
It works like a courtroom.
The null is like 'innocent until proven guilty'.
Only strong evidence lets us reject it. Weak evidence means 'not guilty', which is not the same as 'innocent'.
So, if the coin were fair, how often would we see 9 or more heads in 10 flips?
Picture a fair coin flipped 10 times, over and over.
9 or more heads happens only about 1% of the time.
Before testing, we choose a line, usually 5%.
1% is below it, so we reject the null. The coin is probably rigged.
But 6 heads happens about 38% of the time. Then we'd fail to reject the null, which doesn't prove the coin is fair.
So remember: assume nothing's going on, check how surprising the data is,
and reject that assumption only when the data is really surprising.
Quick quiz!
A company claims its new pill lowers blood pressure.
In a test, what is the null hypothesis?
The pill does nothing!
The null always says there's no effect. The company has to bring enough evidence to reject it.
Next: that 1% has a name. The p-value.
Follow for data science made simple!
